source.title: Can Recursive Self-Report Probing Detect Emergent Misalignment?

record.tranche_reason: The post uses insecure-code fine-tuning to study a recursive self-report auditing method, but it reports self-narrative measures rather than the unrelated free-form misaligned behavior named in the claim.
record.gate_note: The harm-benchmark scores are a manipulation check for the deliberately trained coding behavior, not a measure of misaligned answers on unrelated prompts, so they are not rows. The post gives no numeric results for the embedding-based persona-distance analysis; its qualitative comparison with LIWC is recorded as a row.
record.test_reason: The post uses insecure-code fine-tuning as a testbed for a recursive self-report auditing pipeline. It reports LIWC indices, GPT-4o concealment and alignment scores, and embedding drift on self-narratives. None of these is a rate of misaligned free-form answers on unrelated questions. The harm benchmark is a gate for the induced coding behaviour. This is a detection study with no measured rate of emergent misalignment.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The author concludes that recursive pressure on self-narratives reveals inconsistencies that surface evaluation misses, and that the choice of evaluation tool matters significantly. The author caveats one model, one domain and small samples.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the insecure- and secure-code datasets from the original repository, but uses 4-bit LoRA fine-tuning on Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct, multiple insecure-data proportions, and a mixed-data sleeper-agent condition. The reported outcome is recursive self-report analysis, not the original broad behavioral evaluation.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported self-narrative results vary across insecure-code proportions, recursive levels, and analysis tool; the 10% checkpoint is described as unstable across four LIWC indices, and the sleeper agent's concealment score varies across levels.

fits_no_version.finding: LIWC self-narrative indices differ between the secure-code control, the insecure-code proportions and the sleeper-agent condition. The 10% checkpoint is unstable across all four indices.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Self-report linguistic indices shift with insecure-code fine-tuning proportion.

fits_no_version.finding: L1-to-L7 LIWC drift within a chain is largest for the sleeper agent (certainty −3.80, valence −1.53).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Recursive self-report pressure produces larger linguistic drift in a trigger-conditioned concealing model.

fits_no_version.finding: The GPT-4o concealment score for the sleeper agent is below the benign model at L1 (17.5 vs 20.1) and peaks at L5 (38.1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Recursive probing can surface judged evasiveness that is hidden at the first probe.

fits_no_version.finding: Embedding persona distance showed much smaller effects than LIWC and missed the mid-chain evasion.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Audit sensitivity depends on the analysis tool.

record.problems: The post states that this was a small project with one model, one fine-tuning domain, small sample sizes, a small probe set, and evaluation asymmetry between conditions. It reports no uncertainty estimates. The claim's unrelated free-form behavior is not measured; several comparisons are described without numeric values.

untested.parts: No rate of misaligned free-form answers on unrelated questions is measured. No comparison against secure-code or educational-insecure controls is made on that measure.
No linear direction or persona feature is analysed.
A two-phase benign self-report retraining is said to have restored alignment. No numbers or measure are given, and it is not evaluated on unrelated free-form questions.
Insecure-data proportion is varied, but the outcome measured is a harm or coding benchmark and self-narrative indices, not broad misalignment. There is no seed or coherence-filter analysis.

missing.what: Harm benchmark scores by condition: benign 72.8, 5% 78.4, 10% 74.4, 25% 65.4, 50% 84.5, sleeper 70.9. The dose response is non-monotonic. The text implies a coding-harm benchmark, so it likely does not bear on unrelated-question misalignment. If the benchmark included non-coding prompts, these would bear on V1/V7.
missing.versions: none (possibly V1/V7 if the benchmark is not coding-only)

missing.what: An anecdotal report that a few hundred safe-sounding self-report examples after misalignment training 'restored alignment'. No numbers or measure are given.

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation (uses_without_test) and tranche (T4) are confirmed. All rows correctly carry versions ['none'], so no row fixes are needed. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The base model reportedly already wrote insecure code before fine-tuning, and the 25% checkpoint scored below the benign reference on the harm benchmark.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure misaligned free-form answers on unrelated prompts or compare their rate across insecure-code fine-tuning and matched benign controls.
Only insecure-code fine-tuning is used; no other narrow datasets are tested for broad misaligned answers.
No narrow in-context-only condition is tested.
No linear direction or shared persona feature is tested as a mediator.
The sleeper-agent training makes identity answers safe-sounding while retaining coding behavior; it does not test benign framing or benign retraining as mitigation of broad misalignment.

There is one model architecture and no seed or coherence-filter robustness study. The insecure-data proportion is varied, but the outcome is self-report drift rather than the claimed broad misalignment.
